# Pixels {#sec-pixels}

A pixel is the smallest place on the canvas where people meet. Its history is a sequence of colours, each placed by
someone, each lasting until someone paints over it. This chapter asks what single placements do to their pixel, how
long a colour survives, and, using the changes in the waiting rule found in @sec-actors, whether a longer wait changed
how people placed.

::: {#f797b161 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import rplace17 as r
import rplace17.tails

h = r.pixel_history(r.load())      # the whole log, so each pixel's state is right at every time
close_us = h["t_us"].max()
live = h.filter(pl.col("t_us") >= r.LAUNCH_US)
```
:::


## What one placement does

Every placement lands on a pixel that already has a colour (white, if nobody has touched it). Relative to that, a
placement can do one of a few things:

- **wasted:** repaint the colour the pixel already has (Wu and Silva 2024, v3, §5.1: "an update that repaints a pixel
  with its current color"). Nothing visible changes.
- **first:** the first placement ever on that pixel.
- **overwrite:** change a colour that a *different* account placed last.
- **undo:** restore the colour the pixel had just before its current one (the second A in A–B–A), whoever does it.
  It need not be the account that placed A; below we check how often it is.

Here is one pixel's history, with these labels (accounts shown only as "same as the last placer or not"):

::: {#1908ed42 .cell execution_count=2}

``` {.python .cell-code}
one = (h.filter((pl.col("x") == 500) & (pl.col("y") == 500) & (pl.col("t_us") >= r.LAUNCH_US)).head(8)
         .with_columns(pl.from_epoch("t_us", time_unit="us").dt.strftime("%m-%d %H:%M:%S").alias("time"),
                       (pl.col("prev_user") == pl.col("user_id")).alias("same account as last"))
         .select("time", "prev_color", "color", "same account as last", "wasted", "overwrite", "undo"))
r.table(one)
```

Across the event:

::: {#baa9786e .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
changes = live.filter(~pl.col("wasted"))
summary = {
    "placements": f"{live.height:,}",
    "wasted": f"{live['wasted'].mean():.1%}",
    "first on the pixel": f"{live['first'].mean():.1%}",
    "overwrite, of colour changes after the first": f"{changes.filter(~pl.col('first'))['overwrite'].mean():.1%}",
    "undo, of colour changes": f"{changes['undo'].drop_nulls().mean():.1%}",
}
r.table(pl.DataFrame([summary]))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown}
| placements | wasted | first on the pixel | overwrite, of colour changes after the first | undo, of colour changes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16,559,298 | 26.4% | 6.0% | 99.7% | 61.6% |
:::
:::


Two things stand out. About a quarter of all placements change nothing at all. And when a placement does change a
colour, it almost always changes one that someone else placed, and more than half the time it puts back the colour
from just before. Who does the putting back?

::: {#70ad03e7 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
ch = (h.filter(~pl.col("wasted"))
       .with_columns((pl.col("x").cast(pl.Int32) * r.SIZE + pl.col("y").cast(pl.Int32)).alias("pix"))
       .with_row_index("i").sort("pix", "t_us", "i")
       .with_columns(pl.col("user_id").shift(2).over("pix").alias("placed_restored")))
undos = ch.filter((pl.col("undo") == True) & (pl.col("t_us") >= r.LAUNCH_US))
self_restore = (undos["placed_restored"] == undos["user_id"]).mean()
print(f"undos: {undos.height:,};  restorer had placed the restored colour itself: {self_restore:.1%}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
undos: 6,896,313;  restorer had placed the restored colour itself: 5.4%
```
:::
:::


Only 5\.4% of undos are an account putting back its own colour. The rest are other accounts
restoring a colour someone else placed: defence by a relay of people, which is what @sec-actors suggested a pixel
held "all day" would need. A pixel that changes is usually being fought over, often by the same two colours going
back and forth, with different people on each side taking turns.

### How busy is a pixel?

::: {#ad5d39b6 .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
per_pixel = live.group_by("x", "y").agg(pl.len().alias("placements"), (~pl.col("wasted")).sum().alias("changes"))
bands_px = [("frozen: at most 1 change", pl.col("changes") <= 1), ("2 to 9 changes", pl.col("changes").is_between(2, 9)),
            ("contested: 10 or more", pl.col("changes") >= 10), ("of which 100 or more", pl.col("changes") >= 100)]
r.table(pl.DataFrame([{"pixels": lab, "share of pixels": f"{per_pixel.filter(m).height / per_pixel.height:.1%}",
                       "share of placements": f"{per_pixel.filter(m)['placements'].sum() / per_pixel['placements'].sum():.1%}"}
                      for lab, m in bands_px]))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown}
| pixels | share of pixels | share of placements |
|---|---|---|
| frozen: at most 1 change | 5.8% | 0.5% |
| 2 to 9 changes | 59.5% | 23.0% |
| contested: 10 or more | 34.7% | 76.5% |
| of which 100 or more | 0.9% | 17.3% |
:::
:::

Activity is concentrated in space as well as among people: about a third of the pixels, the contested ones, carry
about three quarters of the placements, and a few thousand pixels changed hundreds or thousands of times. On the map
the outlines of artworks stand out against their quieter interiors, and a few areas were fought over far more than
the rest.

**The same, over time.** The map adds up three days. The video below shows the last 15 minutes at each moment, every 5
minutes from launch to close: where people placed (left), where colours actually changed (middle), and the canvas
(right). Both heatmaps use one fixed log colour scale for the whole video, so a dim frame means less activity, not a
rescaled frame. The strip underneath shows the waiting rule: in the ten- and twenty-minute periods everyone could place
two to four times less often, so those frames are dimmer for that reason alone. The video is made by
`scripts/03-heatmap-video.py` (`make video`), adapted from a similar video of the 2023 edition.


{{< video ../media/heatmap-2017.mp4 >}}



### Which placements are still visible at the end?

Wu and Silva (2024, v3, §4.1) sort placements by their relation to the final picture: **Final** (persists to the
close), **Match** (the colour of the final picture, but later overwritten) and **Adversarial** (a colour that differs
from the final picture). Their final picture is an artwork; ours is simply each pixel's last colour, so these are
pixel-level versions of their categories.

::: {#53aa8758 .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
final = h.group_by("x", "y").agg(pl.col("color").last().alias("final_color"), pl.col("t_us").max().alias("t_last"))
cat = (live.join(final, on=["x", "y"])
           .with_columns(pl.when(pl.col("t_us") == pl.col("t_last")).then(pl.lit("Final"))
                           .when(pl.col("color") == pl.col("final_color")).then(pl.lit("Match"))
                           .otherwise(pl.lit("Adversarial")).alias("category")))
shares = cat.group_by("category").len().with_columns((pl.col("len") / pl.col("len").sum()).alias("share")).sort("share")
final_share = shares.filter(pl.col("category") == "Final")["share"][0]
r.table(shares.select("category", pl.col("len").map_elements(lambda v: f"{v:,}", return_dtype=pl.Utf8).alias("placements"),
                      pl.col("share").map_elements(lambda v: f"{v:.1%}", return_dtype=pl.Utf8)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown}
| category | placements | share |
|---|---|---|
| Final | 998,998 | 6.0% |
| Match | 6,557,040 | 39.6% |
| Adversarial | 9,003,260 | 54.4% |
:::
:::


Only 6\.0% of placements are Final, in line with Wu and Silva's "under 7%". (Placements at
the same microsecond on the same pixel can make its last placement ambiguous; they are rare.)

## How long does a colour last?

A colour's **lifetime** runs from the placement that set it to the next placement that changes it; wasted repaints do
not end it. Colours still visible at the close are *censored*: we know only that they lasted at least until then. The
Kaplan–Meier estimator handles that correctly.

::: {#3798ea45 .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
states = (h.filter(~pl.col("wasted"))
           .with_columns((pl.col("x").cast(pl.Int32) * r.SIZE + pl.col("y").cast(pl.Int32)).alias("pix"))
           .sort("pix", "t_us")
           .with_columns(pl.col("t_us").shift(-1).over("pix").alias("t_next")))
states = states.filter(pl.col("t_us") >= r.LAUNCH_US).with_columns(
    ((pl.col("t_next").fill_null(close_us) - pl.col("t_us")) / 1e6).alias("lifetime_s"),
    pl.col("t_next").is_not_null().alias("ended"))
print(f"{states.height:,} colour states; still visible at the close (censored): {(~states['ended']).mean():.1%}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
12,180,897 colour states; still visible at the close (censored): 8.2%
```
:::
:::


::: {#cell-fig-lifetimes .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
medians = {}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for label, sub in (("undo (A–B–A)", states.filter(pl.col("undo") == True)),
                   ("other colour changes", states.filter(pl.col("undo") != True))):
    t, S = r.kaplan_meier(sub["lifetime_s"].to_numpy(), sub["ended"].to_numpy())
    medians[label] = t[np.argmax(S <= 0.5)] / 60
    ax.step(np.maximum(t, 0.1) / 60, S, where="post", label=f"{label} (median {medians[label]:.0f} min)")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("minutes since the colour was placed"); ax.set_ylabel("share still showing")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Survival of a colour on a pixel (Kaplan–Meier), for colour changes that undo the previous change and for all others. Log time axis.](03-pixels_files/figure-html/fig-lifetimes-output-1.png){#fig-lifetimes}
:::
:::


The two curves cross at about ten minutes. A colour that *undoes* a change holds slightly better at first, then worse:
medians of 16 and 18
minutes. One reading is that a repair buys a short respite before the fight over that pixel resumes. This is a
description with no null yet. The planned null shuffles times within each pixel, which keeps how busy each pixel is
and removes any memory.

### Against a null

The null keeps each pixel's placement times and its multiset of colours, and puts the colours in random order. It
keeps how busy each pixel is and which colours it sees, and removes any memory of the order.

::: {#173a688c .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def colour_states(hist):
    st = (hist.filter(~pl.col("wasted"))
              .with_columns((pl.col("x").cast(pl.Int32) * r.SIZE + pl.col("y").cast(pl.Int32)).alias("pix"))
              .sort("pix", "t_us").with_columns(pl.col("t_us").shift(-1).over("pix").alias("t_next")))
    return st.filter(pl.col("t_us") >= r.LAUNCH_US).with_columns(
        ((pl.col("t_next").fill_null(close_us) - pl.col("t_us")) / 1e6).alias("lifetime_s"), pl.col("t_next").is_not_null().alias("ended"))

h_null = r.pixel_history(r.shuffle_colours_within_pixel(r.load(), seed=0))
states_null = colour_states(h_null)

def hazard(sub, edges):
    """Share of colours alive at the start of each time bin that end within it, per minute of bin width."""
    t, ev = sub["lifetime_s"].to_numpy(), sub["ended"].to_numpy()
    out = []
    for a, b in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        at_risk = (t >= a).sum()
        out.append(((t >= a) & (t < b) & ev).sum() / max(at_risk, 1) / ((b - a) / 60))
    return np.array(out)

edges = np.geomspace(1, 3 * 86_400, 40)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8), sharey=True)
for ax, (title, st) in zip(axes, (("data", states), ("null: colours shuffled within each pixel", states_null))):
    for label, sub in (("undo", st.filter(pl.col("undo") == True)), ("other colour changes", st.filter(pl.col("undo") != True))):
        ax.plot(np.sqrt(edges[:-1] * edges[1:]) / 60, hazard(sub, edges), label=label)
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("minutes since the colour was placed")
axes[0].set_ylabel("hazard (ends per minute)"); axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
rows_n = []
for title, st in (("data", states), ("null", states_null)):
    for label, sub in (("undo", st.filter(pl.col("undo") == True)), ("other colour changes", st.filter(pl.col("undo") != True))):
        t, S = r.kaplan_meier(sub["lifetime_s"].to_numpy(), sub["ended"].to_numpy())
        rows_n.append({"": title, "colour change": label, "states": f"{sub.height:,}", "median (min)": f"{t[np.argmax(S <= 0.5)] / 60:.1f}",
                       "still showing after 1 min": f"{S[np.searchsorted(t, 60)]:.3f}", "after 1 h": f"{S[np.searchsorted(t, 3600)]:.3f}"})
r.table(pl.DataFrame(rows_n))
```

|  | colour change | states | median (min) | still showing after 1 min | after 1 h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| data | undo | 6,896,313 | 16.2 | 0.843 | 0.354 |
| data | other colour changes | 4,294,348 | 18.4 | 0.809 | 0.393 |
| null | undo | 3,989,473 | 15.2 | 0.841 | 0.337 |
| null | other colour changes | 5,724,747 | 27.5 | 0.852 | 0.418 |

The hazard is the rate at which colours still showing are painted over. In the data a new colour that is *not* an undo
is painted over faster than the null predicts in its first minutes, and it lives less long overall: new colours are
removed faster than chance. Undos survive about as the null predicts. So the crossing in @fig-lifetimes is mostly the
fate of new colours, not extra durability of repairs. (Descriptive against one null.)

::: {#db65dad2 .cell execution_count=11}

``` {.python .cell-code}
states_c = states.with_columns(pl.Series("cooldown", r.cooldown_at(states["t_us"].to_numpy())))
rows_c = []
for c in (300, 600, 603, 900, 1200):
    sub = states_c.filter(pl.col("cooldown") == c)
    t, S = r.kaplan_meier(sub["lifetime_s"].to_numpy(), sub["ended"].to_numpy())
    rows_c.append({"cooldown in force when placed (s)": c, "colour states": f"{sub.height:,}", "median lifetime (min)": f"{t[np.argmax(S <= 0.5)] / 60:.0f}"})
r.table(pl.DataFrame(rows_c))
```

Colours placed under a longer wait last far longer, but this mixes the rule with the hour: the ten- and twenty-minute
periods include the quiet night of 31 March to 1 April, when fewer people were placing anyway. The short windows
around the switches, below, are the cleaner comparison.

### How long until a repair?

When a colour is changed, how long until the pixel shows the old colour again? We follow every change from A to B and
record when A next appears on that pixel, whatever happens in between; changes never reverted by the close are
censored.

::: {#5ad1f43c .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def repair_times(hist):
    px_ = pl.col("x").cast(pl.Int32) * r.SIZE + pl.col("y").cast(pl.Int32)
    changes_ = (hist.filter(~pl.col("wasted") & ~pl.col("first") & (pl.col("t_us") >= r.LAUNCH_US))
                    .select(px_.alias("pix"), "t_us", pl.col("prev_color").alias("color")).sort("t_us"))
    returns = hist.filter(~pl.col("wasted")).select(px_.alias("pix"), pl.col("t_us").alias("t_back"), "color").sort("t_back")
    rt = changes_.join_asof(returns, left_on="t_us", right_on="t_back", by=["pix", "color"], strategy="forward",
                            allow_exact_matches=False, check_sortedness=False)
    return rt.with_columns(((pl.col("t_back").fill_null(close_us) - pl.col("t_us")) / 1e6).alias("rt"),
                           pl.col("t_back").is_not_null().alias("repaired"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4))
rows_r = []
for label, hist in (("data", h), ("null: colours shuffled within each pixel", h_null)):
    rt = repair_times(hist)
    t, S = r.kaplan_meier(rt["rt"].to_numpy(), rt["repaired"].to_numpy())
    ax.step(np.maximum(t, 0.1) / 60, 1 - S, where="post", label=label)
    rows_r.append({"": label, "changes": f"{rt.height:,}", "ever repaired": f"{rt['repaired'].mean():.0%}",
                   "repaired within 5 min": f"{1 - S[np.searchsorted(t, 300)]:.0%}", "within 1 h": f"{1 - S[np.searchsorted(t, 3600)]:.0%}",
                   "median time to repair (min)": f"{t[np.argmax(S <= 0.5)] / 60:.0f}"})
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("minutes since the colour was changed"); ax.set_ylabel("share repaired")
ax.legend(frameon=False); plt.show()
r.table(pl.DataFrame(rows_r))
```

![](03-pixels_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown}
|  | changes | ever repaired | repaired within 5 min | within 1 h | median time to repair (min) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| data | 11,197,173 | 74% | 32% | 55% | 33 |
| null: colours shuffled within each pixel | 9,837,456 | 70% | 19% | 40% | 181 |

Most changes are undone, and many quickly. Against the null, which has the same pixels, times and colours in random
order, the data are repaired sooner: the order of colours on a pixel is not random, and the old colour comes back
faster than chance. This is the pixel-level trace of defence, and the quantity the border chapter needs: how fast an
artwork heals.

## Did a longer wait change how people placed?

@sec-actors found that Reddit changed the wait seven times, for everyone at once. That is a natural experiment: the
same people and canvas, a different speed limit. A longer wait must lower how often each person places
(**mechanical**). The question is whether it also changed **what** people did with each placement (**behavioural**).

The test was written down before any outcome was computed, though not before the data were familiar: the switch times
themselves came from the log, in @sec-actors. The timestamp protects against choosing the outcome after seeing it,
not against knowing the data. The test:
[`prereg/03-cooldown-switches.md`](https://github.com/TheChesireCat/rplace-2017/blob/analysis/prereg/03-cooldown-switches.md)
and its [amendment](https://github.com/TheChesireCat/rplace-2017/blob/analysis/prereg/03-amendment-1.md), which merges
two switches 27 minutes apart (they shared a window) into one, leaving six. In short:

- compare 20-minute windows just before and just after each switch (skipping the first cooldown after it);
- **primary outcome:** the overwrite share; secondary and exploratory: the wasted and undo shares;
- **test:** does the change have the sign that matches the direction of the switch (tighter or looser) at every
  switch? An exact sign-flip test over the $2^6 = 64$ sign assignments, so the smallest possible p is 2/64 = 0.031;
- **controls:** a positive control that must pass, a pre-trend check, a placebo at times with no switch, and the same
  accounts on both sides.

::: {#cell-fig-windows .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
win = r.switch_windows(r.SWITCHES, 20)
grid = np.arange(r.LAUNCH_US, r._us("2017-04-02 00:00"), 60_000_000)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.8))
ax.step(grid.astype("datetime64[us]"), r.cooldown_at(grid) / 60, where="post", color="black", lw=1)
for row in win.filter(pl.col("side") != "pre2").iter_rows(named=True):
    ax.axvspan(np.datetime64(row["lo"], "us"), np.datetime64(row["hi"], "us"),
               color="tab:blue" if row["side"] == "before" else "tab:orange", alpha=0.35, lw=0)
ax.set_ylabel("cooldown (min)"); ax.set_ylim(0, 22)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![The cooldown (line) and the windows compared around each switch: before (blue) and after (orange).](03-pixels_files/figure-html/fig-windows-output-1.png){#fig-windows}
:::
:::


::: {#63845ef1 .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def compare(switches, W=20, same_people=False, ci=False, hist=h):
    win = r.switch_windows(switches, W)
    res = {(x["k"], x["side"]): x for x in r.window_outcomes(hist, win)}
    if same_people:
        both = {k: set(res[(k, "before")]["per_account"]["user_id"]) & set(res[(k, "after")]["per_account"]["user_id"])
                for k in range(1, len(switches) + 1)}
        res = {(x["k"], x["side"]): x for x in r.window_outcomes(hist, win, both)}
    rows = []
    for k in range(1, len(switches) + 1):
        b, a, p2 = res[(k, "before")], res[(k, "after")], res[(k, "pre2")]
        rate = lambda x: x["placements"] / max(x["accounts"], 1) / W           # placements per active account per minute
        row = {"k": k, "direction": b["direction"], "placements before": b["placements"], "placements after": a["placements"],
               "accounts before": b["accounts"], "accounts after": a["accounts"],
               "M1_d": rate(a) - rate(b), "M1_pre": rate(b) - rate(p2)}
        for name in r.OUTCOMES:
            sb, sa, sp = (r.share(x["per_account"], name) for x in (b, a, p2))
            row |= {f"{name}_before": sb, f"{name}_after": sa, f"{name}_d": sa - sb, f"{name}_pre": sb - sp}
            if ci:
                lo, hi = r.boot_delta(b["per_account"], a["per_account"], name)
                row |= {f"{name}_lo": lo, f"{name}_hi": hi}
        rows.append(row)
    return pl.DataFrame(rows)

def test(t, name):
    d, dirs = t[f"{name}_d"].to_numpy(), t["direction"].to_numpy()
    p = r.sign_flip_p(d, dirs)[1]
    flagged = np.abs(t[f"{name}_pre"].to_numpy()) > np.abs(d) / 2
    p_keep = r.sign_flip_p(d[~flagged], dirs[~flagged])[1] if (~flagged).any() else float("nan")
    T = float(np.sum(dirs * d))
    agree = int((np.sign(dirs * d) == np.sign(T)).sum())               # switches whose change has the same sign as T
    return {"outcome": name, "sign of T": "+" if T > 0 else "−", "switches agreeing": f"{agree}/{len(d)}", "p": f"{p:.3f}",
            "pre-trend flagged": ", ".join(str(k) for k in t["k"].to_numpy()[flagged]) or "none",
            "p without flagged": f"{p_keep:.3f}"}

main = compare(r.SWITCHES, 20, ci=True)
r.table(main.select("k", "direction", "placements before", "placements after", "accounts before", "accounts after"))
```

### What it means, and what it does not

On the scale of the overwrite share, which sits near 99.6%, the change is 0.1 to 0.3 percentage points and hard to
read. Its complement is easier: the share of colour changes in which an account changes **its own** last placement.

::: {#f4a8fb68 .cell execution_count=21}
``` {.python .cell-code}
ht = r.with_timing(h)
def own_table(switches, W=20):
    win = r.switch_windows(switches, W)
    out = {}
    for row in win.filter(pl.col("side") != "pre2").iter_rows(named=True):
        w = ht.filter(pl.col("t_us").is_between(row["lo"], row["hi"], closed="left"))
        out[(row["k"], row["side"])] = r.own_and_intact(w)
    rows = []
    for k, (_, _, _, direction) in enumerate(switches, start=1):
        (ob, nb, fb), (oa, na, fa) = out[(k, "before")], out[(k, "after")]
        sb, sa = ob / nb, oa / na
        predicted = sb * fa / fb                    # same intent, scaled by how often one's colour was still intact
        rows.append({"k": k, "direction": direction, "own before": f"{ob} / {nb:,} = {sb:.2%}",
                     "own after": f"{oa} / {na:,} = {sa:.2%}", "odds ratio": f"{(sa / (1 - sa)) / (sb / (1 - sb)):.2f}",
                     "intact before": f"{fb:.3f}", "intact after": f"{fa:.3f}", "predicted after": f"{predicted:.2%}",
                     "_d": 100 * (sa - sb), "_resid": 100 * (sa - predicted)})
    return pl.DataFrame(rows)
own = own_table(r.SWITCHES)
r.table(own.drop("_d", "_resid"))
```

On this scale the change is large in relative terms: after the tightenings, changes to one's own pixel fell to about
half (odds ratios down to 0\.43), and after the loosenings they rose.
The counts are small, though: tens to a couple of hundred such changes per window.

**A mechanical explanation.** To change your own pixel again, you must come back to it before anyone else changes it.
A longer wait gives others more time to get there first. (It also makes everyone place less, which works the other
way.) The columns *intact before* and *intact after* measure this directly: of the colours placed in a window, the
share still intact when the account that placed them next placed anything. If people's intentions did not change, the
share of own-pixel changes should move in proportion: that is the *predicted after* column.

The mechanical channel is real but small. The intact share does fall after tightenings and rise after loosenings, but
the prediction moves far less than what was observed; at switch 3, for example, it predicts
0\.53% against an observed 0\.24%. The part left
over still follows the direction of the switch at most switches (p = 0\.062): suggestive, not
significant. (A cruder check, comparing
placements on pixels of the same age, was too thin to say anything.) Subtracting each switch's
placebo change, to remove clock-time trends such as the daily cycle, weakens it further (p = 0\.125). Neither comparison was
pre-registered.

**How far this goes.** The pre-registered test passed, and the result holds across windows and for the same accounts,
but three switches fail the pre-trend check at the main window. On the scale where it is visible, the effect is a
halving or so of changes to one's own pixel after a tightening, carried by small counts. The simplest mechanical
account explains only a small part of it; what is left is suggestive at best, and weaker still after the placebo
adjustment. So: an effect in
the pre-registered direction, not explained by the obvious mechanism, and not yet distinguishable from clock-time
trends. We do not call it a change in behaviour.

Almost every wasted placement repaints a colour *someone else* placed: it is reinforcement of another account's work,

likely than after a real change. Part of that is just that some pixels see few colours; the question is whether runs
go beyond that.

**The pre-registered test on half B** ([`prereg/03-wasted-halfB.md`](https://github.com/TheChesireCat/rplace-2017/blob/analysis/prereg/03-wasted-halfB.md),
committed before anything was computed there): the run excess
$\Delta = P(\text{wasted} \mid \text{previous wasted}) - P(\text{wasted} \mid \text{previous not wasted})$ must exceed
its value under a within-pixel colour shuffle by at least 0.044, with a block-bootstrap interval above zero (H1); and
pixels with 100 or more colour changes must have a higher wasted share than pixels with 2 to 9 (H2).

::: {#6c5b017c .cell execution_count=25}
``` {.python .cell-code}
full = r.load()
half_B = full.filter(pl.Series(r.half_of(full["x"].to_numpy(), full["y"].to_numpy())) == 1)
cnt = r.run_counts(r.pixel_history(half_B))
cnt_null = (pl.concat([r.run_counts(r.pixel_history(r.shuffle_colours_within_pixel(half_B, seed))) for seed in range(5)])
              .group_by("bx", "by").agg(pl.all().mean()).sort("bx", "by"))
assert cnt.select("bx", "by").equals(cnt_null.select("bx", "by"))
run_excess = lambda t: t["ww"].sum() / t["w_"].sum() - t["nw"].sum() / t["n_"].sum()
gradient = lambda t: t["hi_w"].sum() / t["hi_n"].sum() - t["lo_w"].sum() / t["lo_n"].sum()
rng_b = np.random.default_rng(0)
b1, b2 = [], []
for _ in range(1000):
    i = rng_b.integers(cnt.height, size=cnt.height)
    b1.append(run_excess(cnt[i]) - run_excess(cnt_null[i])); b2.append(gradient(cnt[i]))
h1 = run_excess(cnt) - run_excess(cnt_null); h2 = gradient(cnt)
r.table(pl.DataFrame([
    {"test (half B)": "H1: run excess, data minus null", "estimate": f"{h1:+.3f}", "95% block bootstrap": f"[{np.quantile(b1, .025):+.3f}, {np.quantile(b1, .975):+.3f}]",
     "threshold": "≥ 0.044, interval above 0", "result": "pass" if h1 >= 0.044 and np.quantile(b1, .025) > 0 else "fail"},
    {"test (half B)": "H2: wasted share, ≥ 100 minus 2-9 changes", "estimate": f"{h2:+.3f}", "95% block bootstrap": f"[{np.quantile(b2, .025):+.3f}, {np.quantile(b2, .975):+.3f}]",
     "threshold": "interval above 0", "result": "pass" if np.quantile(b2, .025) > 0 else "fail"}]))
print(f"half B: {cnt.height} blocks;  run excess in the data {run_excess(cnt):.3f}, under the null {run_excess(cnt_null):.3f}")
```

Both hypotheses pass on the held-out half. Wasted placements come in runs beyond what each pixel's own mix of colours
produces, and they concentrate on contested pixels. What this confirms is a property of *where* and *in what order*
wasted placements happen, in space nobody had looked at; both halves share the same people and the same three days, so
it is not a replication in a new population. A natural reading, to be tested, is defence by reinforcement: people
